newsitem.title: CHINA: China police release dissident, keep close watch.
newsitem.headline: China police release dissident, keep close watch.

text.p: Chinese police maintained tight surveillance over veteran dissident Jin Cheng on Tuesday after detaining and releasing him twice in less than a week, the activist's wife said.

Jin, 38, a former official who last week issued a daring call for public justice in the case of a disgraced Beijing leader, was detained from early on Monday until about 10.30 p.m. (1430 GMT), his wife, Liu Xiuli, said by telephone.
"They kept him in custody for 15 hours but did not really speak to him about anything... They just kept him locked up," she said, adding that plainclothes police continued to keep close watch on him.
"They were waiting for him outside and went with him to work," she said.

On Tuesday last week Jin sent an open letter to the head of the National People's Congress, or parliament, calling for former Beijing Communist Party boss Chen Xitong to be punished for prompting a bloody crackdown on pro-democracy protests in 1989.
On Thursday evening Beijing police detained him until about 2 o'clock the following morning.
Jin, who was involved in management at Beijing's International Conference Centre, was jailed after the crackdown on pro-democracy protests in 1989 for publishing an underground magazine.
Appeals and petitions to the communist-led government that touch on sensitive issues are a risky political act in China, which has clamped down hard on dissent in recent years.

Other dissidents in the Chinese capital said on Monday they had been warned to stay out of circulation for several days during a visit by U.S. National Security Adviser Sandy Berger, who arrived on Sunday and is due to leave on Wednesday.
Not all of China's tiny band of pro-democracy activists heeded the order, however.
Dissident Qin Yongmin said on Tuesday he had issued an appeal for a crucial forthcoming Communist Party congress to embrace democratic reforms.
Qin said he had written to Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin, urging county-level elections and lifting of a ban on political debate in the local media before the end of the century.
The 44-year-old former steel worker said he expected repercussions, but was undaunted.
"Danger is unavoidable... but I'm not afraid," Qin said by telephone from his home in the central city of Wuhan.
